name: Two-Phase Commit
intent: Make a change across several databases succeed everywhere or nowhere, by first asking every participant to promise it can commit and only then telling them all to do so.
scenario: Moving money between two banks means debiting one database and crediting another. If the debit commits and the credit fails, money has vanished. Both changes must happen together, or neither.
problem: A single database can make several changes atomic with a transaction. When the data lives in different databases or services, each has its own commit, and any can fail independently. Without coordination you can end up with some participants committed and others not, and no machine can see all the states at once.

howItWorks.title: A coordinator and several participants
howItWorks.text: One node acts as the coordinator for the transaction. The participants are the databases or services that each hold part of the change. The coordinator drives the protocol and records its decisions in a durable log.

howItWorks.title: Phase 1: prepare (the voting phase)
howItWorks.text: The coordinator asks every participant 'can you commit?'. Each participant does the work, writes it to durable storage, takes locks on the data, and replies yes or no. A yes is a binding promise: once a participant says yes, it must be able to commit even if it crashes and restarts.

howItWorks.title: Phase 2: commit or abort
howItWorks.text: If every participant voted yes, the coordinator logs 'commit' and tells everyone to commit. If any voted no (or did not answer in time), it logs 'abort' and tells everyone to roll back. Participants apply the decision, release their locks and acknowledge.

howItWorks.title: The blocking problem
howItWorks.text: A participant that has voted yes cannot decide alone: if the coordinator crashes before announcing its decision, the participant must wait, holding its locks, until the coordinator returns. Other transactions touching the same rows are stuck. This is why two-phase commit can reduce availability.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives and when to accept the cost
howItWorks.text: Sagas give up isolation to avoid long locks, using compensating actions. Consensus-based commit (as in Spanner) replicates the coordinator so it can fail over. Two-phase commit is still used inside databases and for XA transactions, where strong atomicity across a small number of fast, reliable participants is worth the locking.

pros: Participants keep strong isolation: nobody sees half of the change
Conceptually simple and widely supported (XA, distributed SQL)
No compensation logic is needed in the application
cons: Blocking: a coordinator failure can leave participants holding locks
Latency: two rounds of messages and several forced disk writes
Throughput suffers from locks held across network round trips
Poor fit for slow, unreliable or third-party services
whenToUse: A small number of reliable databases that must stay strictly consistent
Inside distributed databases that coordinate commits across shards
When business rules cannot tolerate temporary inconsistency
whenNotToUse: Long-running business processes across many services (use sagas)
Calls to external systems that do not support prepare and commit
Systems that must remain available when the coordinator or a participant is down
pitfalls: A single, unreplicated coordinator that is also a single point of failure
Holding locks while waiting on a slow participant, with no timeout policy
Participants that vote yes without durably storing the promise first
Forgetting recovery: after a crash the coordinator and participants must read their logs and finish the transaction

roles.label: Coordinator
roles.description: Collects votes and announces the decision.

roles.label: Participant
roles.description: Holds part of the data and votes.

roles.label: Durable log
roles.description: Records promises and decisions so they survive crashes.

quiz.question: A coordinator runs a transfer across two bank databases. In the prepare phase database B votes yes and database A votes no. What happens?
options: B commits, because it already promised that it could
The coordinator retries A until A finally votes yes
The coordinator follows the majority and commits
The coordinator aborts and tells both to roll back
quiz.explanation: Commit needs every participant to vote yes. Any no, or no answer, means abort for all, and the yes vote only meant B could commit if told to. There is no majority rule in two-phase commit.

quiz.question: Both participants have voted yes. The coordinator crashes before sending its decision and stays down for 20 minutes. What happens to the participants?
options: They time out after a few seconds and abort on their own
They commit on their own, because both voted yes
They elect a new coordinator among themselves and carry on
They wait with locks held, and other work on those rows blocks
quiz.explanation: A participant that voted yes has promised to commit and cannot choose alone, because the coordinator may have decided either way. So it waits with locks held. This blocking is the main weakness of two-phase commit.

quiz.question: An order flow must update an inventory database, call an external payment provider over REST (no prepare support), and send an email. It can take several seconds. A colleague proposes XA two-phase commit. What is the best design?
options: Two-phase commit with a longer lock timeout on each database
A saga of local transactions with compensating actions
Two-phase commit with a replicated coordinator for failover
Two-phase commit for inventory and payment only, ignoring the email
quiz.explanation: The external API cannot prepare or hold a promise, and holding locks across slow remote calls would hurt availability. A saga commits locally and compensates on failure. A replicated coordinator fixes coordinator failure, not the missing prepare.
